title: Slavery — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 10
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 10 · Student Reader pp. 82–95
bigQuestion: How did the Age of Exploration lead to the development of the slave trade?

missions.name: Slavery
missions.blurb: One quiz for the whole chapter, with questions from each of its seven headed sections and the Big Question at the end. This is the hardest chapter in the book, and the questions follow what it says rather than softening it. The card says which page answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

hi: There had been enslaved people for many years prior
spread the practice of slavery on a vast scale

vs.q: Was slavery something new in the Age of Exploration?
opts: No, people had been enslaved for centuries before it
Yes, the Portuguese invented it in the 1400s
Yes, it began when Columbus reached the Caribbean
No, but it had only ever existed in Europe
vs.why: For centuries people all over the world had enslaved those they conquered. The chapter is careful to say so before it says what changed.

vs.q: What did Europeans do that changed slavery so completely?
opts: Used their power and wealth to spread it on a vast scale
Were the first people anywhere to practise it
Made it legal in countries where it had been banned
Began enslaving people from their own countries
vs.why: Scale is the answer the chapter gives. In doing so, it says, they dramatically changed the lives of millions of people.

hi: enslaved people could own property and marry
were not automatically also enslaved

vs.q: In the Ashanti kingdom of West Africa, what could enslaved people do?
opts: Own property, marry, and go free after a set time
Leave whenever they wished to
Hold any position in the kingdom
Refuse to work if they were not paid anything
vs.why: Slavery was part of African life before Europeans arrived, but it was not the same thing. Among some groups enslaved people had rights.

vs.q: What does the chapter call the most important Ashanti difference?
opts: Children of enslaved people were not enslaved too
Enslaved people were paid for their work
Nobody could be enslaved for more than a year
Only prisoners of war could be enslaved
vs.why: Slavery did not pass down to the next generation. That is the line between what African kingdoms practised and what the Atlantic trade became.

hi: provided a cost-effective answer
this practice was incredibly inhumane

vs.q: The book says enslaving Africans was a cost-effective answer for plantation owners. What does cost-effective mean?
opts: Giving benefits without costing a great deal
Costing more than it is really worth
Paid for by a government rather than an owner
Costing the same every year, whatever happens
vs.why: The word describes how plantation owners thought about it. The chapter uses their word and then, in the very next sentence, gives its own.

vs.q: The chapter calls the practice incredibly inhumane. What does inhumane mean?
opts: Cruel and unacceptable
Unusual and hard to explain
Expensive and wasteful
Illegal in most countries
vs.why: Cruel, unacceptable. The book puts cost-effective and inhumane side by side on purpose: the first is what it was to the owners, the second is what it was.

hi: disease and war, which had largely been brought to the islands by the Europeans
well-suited for growing sugar and other crops

vs.q: Why did Caribbean plantation owners give up their plan to use local people as workers?
opts: Disease and war brought by Europeans had killed many
The local people refused to grow sugar for them
Spanish law forbade them from being made to work
They had all moved inland away from the coast
vs.why: The same collapse as in chapter 5, now driving the next thing that happens. The chapter is clear about who brought the disease and the war.

vs.q: The Caribbean islands had little gold or silver. What were they good for?
opts: Growing sugar and other crops
Building ships from island timber
Catching and salting fish
Mining iron ore and copper
vs.why: Land and climate suited sugar, and experts came from the Canary Islands to help set the plantations up. Sugar is what drives this whole chapter.

hi: The Portuguese were the first Europeans involved in the Atlantic slave trade
The pirates traded these people for food

vs.q: Which Europeans were first involved in the Atlantic slave trade?
opts: The Portuguese
The Dutch
The English
The French
vs.why: Their explorations of the African coast had opened up the sources. When Portugal's power collapsed, the Dutch took over much of this trade along with the spice trade.

vs.q: What happened in 1619 when a Dutch ship anchored in the James River in Virginia?
opts: Captured Africans were traded for food
A new English colony was founded there
The first sugar plantation was started
A Spanish ship was sunk in the river
vs.why: Dutch pirates had taken a shipload of enslaved Africans from a Spanish vessel and needed supplies. This was the first arrival of Africans in the English North American colonies.

hi: one of the forts where captured Africans were imprisoned
transporting 2,500 enslaved people across the Atlantic each year

vs.q: What did Elmina, on the west coast of Africa, become?
opts: A fort where captured Africans were imprisoned
A sugar plantation run by the Dutch
A shipyard where the slave ships were built
A market where spices were exchanged
vs.why: It had been a Portuguese trade center for ivory and gold. As the slave trade grew it became a holding fort, and then the center of the Dutch slave trade.

vs.q: By 1655, how many people were the Dutch transporting across the Atlantic each year?
opts: About 2,500
About 250
About 25,000
About 500
vs.why: Every year. When England seized New Netherland there were five hundred Dutch-speaking Africans living in the colony.

hi: Ships carried items such as iron, guns, gunpowder
These ships carried timber, tobacco, grain, sugar, and rice

vs.q: On the triangle of trade, what did ships carry from Europe to Africa?
opts: Iron, guns, gunpowder, knives, cloth, and beads
Sugar, rice, and tobacco from the Americas
Spices, silk, porcelain, and tea
Gold, silver, ivory, and copper
vs.why: Goods on the first leg, people on the second, and plantation crops on the third. Each leg paid for the next, which is what made the trade so hard to stop.

vs.q: What did the middle leg of the triangle carry?
opts: People taken from Africa to the Americas
Spices brought from the Indian Ocean
Soldiers sent out to guard the colonies
Gold mined in Mexico and in Peru
vs.why: People. That is what the slave trade was inside this neat-sounding triangle, and the third leg carried home the timber, tobacco, grain, sugar and rice they were made to produce.

hi: The trip across the Atlantic Ocean was known as the Middle Passage
treated like cargo, not people

vs.q: What was the Middle Passage?
opts: The voyage across the Atlantic
The march inland to a seaport
The sale at a market in the Americas
The journey from the coast to a plantation
vs.why: The middle leg of the triangle. The chapter calls it a terrible, dehumanizing experience, and the next questions are why.

vs.q: Enslaved people were treated like cargo. What is cargo?
opts: Goods carried by a ship or truck
The crew who sail a ship
The record kept of a voyage
The money paid for a voyage
vs.why: Goods. The book uses the word to make a point: they were treated like cargo, not people, chained on platforms where they could not even turn over.

hi: a space about six feet long and sixteen inches wide
about fifteen percent of enslaved people did not survive the journey

vs.q: How much space was each person given on a slave ship?
opts: About six feet long and sixteen inches wide
About six feet long and six feet wide
About ten feet long and three feet wide
About three feet long and three feet wide
vs.why: Chained in place, unable to turn over, in a hold that rose above a hundred degrees in the tropics, fed rice and water twice a day, for two to four months.

vs.q: About what share of people did not survive the Middle Passage?
opts: About fifteen percent
About one percent
About fifty percent
About ninety percent
vs.why: Historians' estimate. The Atlantic slave trade lasted nearly three hundred years, and European slave traders made about fifty-four thousand voyages.

hi: began paying for indentured servants
the soil was not very good and the winters were cold

vs.q: What is an indentured servant?
opts: Someone owing set years of work for a benefit
Someone who works for wages paid each month
Someone born into a lifetime of service
Someone who owns a small share of a farm
vs.why: A contract for a number of years, in exchange for the passage across the ocean. Southern plantation owners paid for them before they turned to enslaved labor.

vs.q: Why was there little demand for a large labor force in the northeastern colonies?
opts: Poor soil and cold winters suited no cash crop
The Pilgrims and Puritans had banned slavery
The colonies there were too small to need workers
Settlers there lived by trading furs instead
vs.why: No cash crop, no demand for mass labor. The chapter still notes that slavery existed on a small scale in the northern colonies.

hi: became more profitable and efficient than hiring indentured servants
Indigo and cotton cultivation also relied on the labor

vs.q: Why did plantation owners move away from indentured servants?
opts: Buying an enslaved workforce became more profitable
Indentured servants refused to come over any more
A law was passed forbidding the contracts
The servants demanded to be paid in land
vs.why: Healthier servants began living long enough to finish their contracts, and owners had to pay out freedom dues — food, clothing, money, livestock, sometimes land. Enslaving people cost less.

vs.q: The chapter says cotton cultivation relied on enslaved labor. What is cultivation?
opts: The planting, growing, and harvesting of crops
The clearing of forest to make new fields
The sale of a crop at a market
The storing of a crop over winter
vs.why: Growing crops, start to finish. Tobacco, then rice, then cotton and indigo — each new cash crop meant more demand for enslaved workers.

hi: Families were frequently broken up
They could not testify in court

vs.q: What frequently happened to families at the slave market?
opts: They were broken up and sold separately
They were always kept together by law
They were sent back to Africa together
They were given land of their own
vs.why: Children were separated from their parents, and husbands from wives. Owners bid against each other for the people they thought would work best for them.

vs.q: Why could a slaveholder mistreat an enslaved person and get away with it?
opts: Enslaved people could not testify in court
There were no courts in the colonies
Owners were allowed to judge their own cases
The colonies had no laws about slavery
vs.why: No testimony, no case. Many colonies also made it illegal to teach enslaved people to read or write.

hi: watched by a person called an overseer
it survived until the end of the Civil War

vs.q: Who watched enslaved people as they worked in the fields?
opts: An overseer
A magistrate
A plantation clerk
A ship's captain
vs.why: Someone who supervises workers to make sure a job is done properly. Work ran from dawn to nightfall with an hour off in the midday heat.

vs.q: Where and until when did slavery survive in North America?
opts: In the American South, until the Civil War ended
In the northern states, until the Revolution
In Canada, until the end of the 1700s
In the Caribbean islands, until about 1800
vs.why: After the American Revolution slavery was abolished in most northern states, but it spread in the South and lasted until the end of the Civil War in the mid-1800s.

hi: was better for some people than for others
both the heroism of the explorers and the tragedies

vs.q: How did the Age of Exploration lead to the development of the slave trade?
opts: New colonies grew crops that needed huge numbers of workers
Explorers were ordered by their kings to capture people
The Turks closed the Silk Road, so trade moved to Africa
Europeans ran out of workers for their farms at home
vs.why: This is the chapter's Big Question, and it is a chain. Exploration brought colonies; colonies grew sugar, tobacco, rice and cotton; those crops needed enormous labor; the indigenous population had collapsed; so Europeans built a trade in human beings to fill the gap.

vs.q: How does the chapter say we should understand the Age of Exploration?
opts: Both the heroism and the tragedies together
Mainly as the bravery of the explorers
Mainly as a story of trade and money
As something too long ago to judge
vs.why: The book's own last word. It says the image of a ship sailing proudly across the Atlantic is much less inspiring when we remember that many of these ships carried human cargo in inhumane conditions.

ageold.title: Age-Old Practice — what was old, and what was new
text: There had been enslaved people for many years prior to the Age of Exploration. For centuries people throughout the world had enslaved those they had conquered. But Europeans used their power and wealth to spread the practice of slavery on a vast scale. In doing so, they dramatically changed the lives of millions of people.
Slavery was part of African life long before Europeans arrived.

But among some groups, enslaved people had rights. For example, in the Ashanti kingdom of West Africa, enslaved people could own property and marry, and they got their freedom after working for a set amount of time. Most importantly, children born to Ashanti-enslaved people were not automatically also enslaved.

americas.title: Slavery in the Americas — sugar, and who was made to grow it
vocab: providing benefits without costing a great deal of money
text: The islands of the Caribbean were not rich in mineral wealth. The land and climate, however, were well-suited for growing sugar and other crops. Experts from the Canary Islands came to Hispaniola and other islands to help the Spanish set up sugar plantations.

These plantations needed an inexpensive labor force. At first, plantation owners planned to use local people to work on the plantations. But disease and war, which had largely been brought to the islands by the Europeans, killed many indigenous people.
As had been the case in the Azores and the Canary Islands, enslaved people from Africa provided a cost-effective answer. However, this practice was incredibly inhumane, and caused much suffering.

trade10.title: The Slave Trade — who ran it, and how it reached Virginia
text: The Portuguese were the first Europeans involved in the Atlantic slave trade. Their explorations of the African coast had opened
up new sources for people they could enslave. When Portugal's power collapsed and the Dutch took over the spice trade, they took over much of the Atlantic slave trade as well.

In 1619, a Dutch ship sailed into the mouth of the James River in the English colony of Virginia in North America and dropped anchor. On board were Dutch pirates who had been attacking other ships on the high seas. They had captured a shipload of enslaved Africans from a Spanish vessel heading for the Caribbean. Now the Dutch sailors were traveling north and needed supplies. The pirates traded these people for food. This was the first arrival of Africans in the English North American colonies.

elmina.title: The Slave Trade — Elmina
text: One of the trade centers the Dutch had taken from the Portuguese was Elmina on the west coast of Africa (in present-day Ghana). For years, Elmina had been a Portuguese trade center where ivory

and gold were exchanged. As the slave trade increased, Elmina became one of the forts where captured Africans were imprisoned before being transported to Europe or to the Americas. Before long, Elmina was the center of the Dutch slave trade.
By 1655, the Dutch were transporting 2,500 enslaved people across the Atlantic each year. When England seized control of New Netherland, there were five hundred Dutch-speaking Africans in the colony.

triangle.title: The Slave Trade — the three legs of the triangle
text: The slave trade was one side of a trading triangle. One segment of the triangle carried goods from Europe to Africa. Ships carried items such as iron, guns, gunpowder, knives, cloth, and beads. Another segment transported people from Africa to the Caribbean islands and later to the English colonies in North America.
And another segment of the triangle made a return trip to Europe. These ships carried timber, tobacco, grain, sugar, and rice from the plantations of the Americas.

middle.title: Middle Passage — the crossing
vocab: goods transported by a ship, plane, or truck
text: The trip across the Atlantic Ocean was known as the Middle Passage. It was a terrible, dehumanizing experience.

ships usually carried between 150 and six hundred Africans. Enslaved people were treated like cargo, not people. They were chained on platforms. Each person had a space about six feet long and sixteen inches wide. Because they were chained in place, they could not even turn over.

The trip across the ocean took between two and four months depending on the weather and the destination. Illness and death were common occurrences. With people packed in close quarters, disease spread easily. Historians estimate that about fifteen percent of enslaved people did not survive the journey.

north.section: The Growth of Slavery in the Colonies
north.title: The Growth of Slavery in the Colonies — north and south
vocab: a person who owes an employer a certain amount of work for a certain amount of time in exchange for some benefit
to send goods to sell in another country
text: In the colonies of North America, the demand for enslaved people came later in the slave trade. The Pilgrims and Puritans settled the colonies in the Northeast where the soil was not very good and the winters were cold. These conditions were not ideal for growing cash crops, so there was no need for a large labor force. Even so, slavery did exist on a small scale in these northern colonies.

In the South, the situation was different. Plantation owners who lived in the southern colonies grew tobacco to export to Europe. They needed many workers to run these plantations. To find a supply of workers, plantation owners began paying for indentured servants to come to the colonies from Europe. In return, the servants agreed to work for a certain number of years.

shift.section: The Growth of Slavery in the Colonies
shift.title: The Growth of Slavery in the Colonies — why it changed
vocab: the planting, growing, and harvesting of crops
text: Freedom dues were what a servant received for completing his or her contract. According to the contract, an indentured servant was given food, clothing, money, and some livestock. Those who were given land could finish their contracts and start farming next door.

Before long, buying an enslaved workforce from Africa became more profitable and efficient than hiring indentured servants. Slavery spread in the 1700s. Millions of acres were planted with tobacco. Planters also introduced a new cash crop, rice, which needed lots of labor to plant and harvest.
In the late 1700s and 1800s, cotton became a third cash crop grown in the American South. Indigo and cotton cultivation also relied on the labor of enslaved people.

plantation10.title: Plantation Life — what the law allowed
text: The life of an enslaved person was very hard. People were sold as slaves at a market where owners bid against each other. Slaveholders bought the people they thought would work best for them. Families were frequently broken up; children were separated from their parents, and husbands from wives.
On the plantation, enslaved people had no freedom. They had to do what their masters told them to do and could not travel

anywhere without permission. They could not testify in court, so an owner could mistreat an enslaved person and get away with it. Many colonies also had laws that made it illegal to teach enslaved people to read or write.

overseer.title: Plantation Life — the work, and how long it lasted
vocab: someone who supervises workers to make sure a job is done properly
text: Enslaved people worked from dawn to nightfall, with an hour off midday in the heat. The work was hard. They worked in the cotton, rice, indigo, and tobacco fields. They chopped wood, built fences, cleared roads, and dug wells. All the while, they were watched by a person called an overseer.

Not all Africans in the colonies were enslaved. Some managed to gain their freedom. A few slaveholders even gave freedom to their enslaved workers. Free Africans in the colonies made their living as farmers and crafts workers. After the American Revolution, slavery was abolished in most of the northern states. But slavery spread in the American South, where it survived until the end of the Civil War in the mid-nineteenth century.

summing.section: Summing Up the Age of Exploration
summing.title: Summing Up — both halves of the story
text: To have a full and well-balanced understanding of the Age of Exploration, we have to recognize that this age, like most ages, was better for some people than for others. Some people made their fortunes; others did not survive perilous journeys.

But for many people, the Age of Exploration was a time of great hardship. Contact with Europeans devastated the indigenous peoples of the Americas. Many died in battle, and disease killed millions more. For millions of Africans, contact with Europeans meant a lifetime of slavery. The image of a ship sailing proudly across the Atlantic becomes much less inspiring when we remember that many of these ships carried human cargo in inhumane conditions. An understanding of the age must include both the heroism of the explorers and the tragedies that resulted from exploration.
